analytic.title: Three Preemption Approaches towards EDF Scheduling for Homogeneous Multiprocessors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: When scheduling a set of real-time tasks, researchers can choose between preemptive and non-preemptive algorithms. However, these algorithms each have their own advantages and drawbacks, necessitating specific analysis in different contexts. In contrast to these two extremes, researchers have proposed the concept of limited-preemption algorithms. Such limited-preemption algorithms serve as feasible alternatives to the former two approaches. Currently, research on this algorithm is based on a homogenous computing environment.

In this paper, we investigate the fixed-preemption point method in limited-preemption algorithms. We compare the impact of limited-preemption EDF algorithm on the performance of homogenous multiprocessors under different fixed-preemption strategies. We introduce a preemptive strategy where highpriority tasks can only be preempted at the most suitable fixedpreemption points, and we provide an effective schedulability analysis for this strategy. The EDF scheduling algorithm based on the best-fit fixed preemption strategy is called the Best Preemptive EDF(BP-EDF). We have introduced an effective schedulability analysis for BP-EDF. Experimental results indicate that the strategy with the most suitable fixed-preemption points demonstrates superior schedulability compared to the other two strategies. Furthermore, its performance in terms of task preemption frequency closely approaches that of the strategy employing fixed-preemption at the lowest priority points.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Whether to preempt is an important factor to consider when implementing scheduling algorithms. Traditional preemptive strategies include fully preemptive and non-preemptive approaches. In a fully preemptive scheduling, the task currently executing can be interrupted by a higher-priority task at any time. The preempted task resumes execution once all This work is supported by the Central guidance for Local scientific and technological development funds (No. YDZJSX20231B001 and YDZJSX20231C001) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62006146 and 62003200) higher-priority tasks are completed. This constitutes a fully preemptive scheduling. The ability of an operating system to immediately allocate the processor to a more urgent task is due to its support for preemption. On the other hand, nonpreemptive scheduling does not allow tasks to be preempted.

Fully preemptive scheduling exhibits better schedulability. However, due to the migration latency and overhead of context switching caused by preemption, it increases the operational overhead of the algorithm. Non-preemptive scheduling enhances system predictability by disabling preemption, yet it results in increased blocking time for high-priority tasks. Both strategies have their own pros and cons. In real-time scheduling, a flexible application of preemptive strategies can effectively balance the requirements of system performance and predictability [1].

In addition to the aforementioned two preemptive strategies, another option is limited-preemption scheduling. Limitedpreemption scheduling involves supporting preemption but with constraints on when preemption can occur. Buttazzo et al. extensively discussed and compared various limitedpreemption scheduling algorithms [2]. The study mentions methods such as preemption thresholds, fixed-preemption points, and delayed preemption. The first method involves assigning a preemption threshold parameter to tasks. Preemption can only occur if the priority of a high-priority task surpasses the preemption threshold of another task. The second method is to set fixed-preemption points for tasks, allowing preemption only when the point is reached during execution. The third method sets a maximum interval where preemption is not allowed for tasks, permitting preemption only after this interval elapses following task execution. Dong [9].

In previous studies of limited-preemption scheduling algorithms with fixed-preemption points, two preemptive allocation strategies have been employed: eager and lazy. Under the eager preemptive strategy, high-priority tasks preempt at the nearest fixed-preemption point. Under the lazy preemptive strategy, high-priority tasks preempt at the nearest fixedpreemption point of the lowest-priority task. We consider an alternative approach of selecting the most suitable fixedpreemption point for preemption. First, we assess whether preemption would cause low-priority tasks to miss their deadlines. Then, among the eligible fixed-preemption points, we choose the nearest one for preemption.

In recent years, the demand for computing power has been continuously increasing, especially for applications like highquality, low-latency live streaming services in vehicles, which require significant processing capabilities [10]- [13]. This demand for computing power has driven the rapid development of parallel computing technology, making multiprocessor systems the prevailing computing platform. Many researchers have begun to explore multiprocessor systems, and currently, most of the research on task scheduling algorithms is based on homogeneous computing environments. Homogeneous multiprocessor systems refer to the use of processors within a computer system that share the same processor architecture or type, typically featuring identical processor models. In such systems, these processors are similar, allowing them to execute the same type of instruction sets and possess comparable performance characteristics and functionalities. This type of system is often employed to enhance computational performance, increase system availability and fault tolerance, as well as balance workloads. Homogeneous multiprocessor systems are commonly compared to heterogeneous multiprocessor systems, which consist of processors with varying architectures or types. Homogeneous systems are more manageable due to the minimal differences among processors, but in certain cases, heterogeneous systems may better fulfill specific performance requirements.

In this paper, we investigate the preemptive strategies of limited-preemption scheduling with fixed-preemption points on a homogeneous multiprocessor platform. All three strategies do not alter the fundamental task priority assignment strategy of the EDF scheduling algorithm; rather, they impose restrictions on the preemption behavior during scheduling. The EP-EDF scheduling algorithm involves highpriority tasks preempting at the nearest fixed-preemption point. The BP-EDF scheduling algorithm allows high-priority tasks to preempt at the nearest fixed-preemption point without affecting the scheduling of lower-priority tasks. The LP-EDF scheduling algorithm enables high-priority tasks to preempt at the nearest fixed-preemption point of the lowest-priority task. We propose a schedulability test for BP-EDF. Our main contributions are as follows:

• We propose a BP-EDF scheduling algorithm that preempts tasks at appropriate fixed points, and we introduce a schedulability test for the BP-EDF algorithm. • Comparison of the EDF algorithms with three different preemptive strategies was conducted, and the superiority of BP-EDF was verified through experiments. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the system model and introduces the three preemptive strategies. Section III derives the schedulability test for the BP-EDF algorithm. Section IV provides a comparative analysis of the three preemptive strategies through experiments. Section V concludes the paper.

The sporadic real-time task τ i = (E i , D i , T i ) is characterized by three parameters, with the task set denoted as Ω. E i represents the execution time on the slowest processor, D i denotes the relative deadline, and T i stands for the period. Ω is a constrained set, hence the presence of E i ≤ D i ≤ T i . When D i = T i , it signifies an implicit deadline system. τ i,j signifies the jth job of task τ i , a i,j represents the arrival time, and f i,j denotes the completion time. The absolute deadline of τ i,j is d i,j = a i,j + D i . d i,j denotes the latest moment of completion for τ i,j . If t ∈ (a i,j , f i,j ) exists, a job is said to be ready at time t.

div.head: B. Interference, workload and time division
div.p: In multiprocessor systems, the parallel execution of tasks leads to mutual influences among them. Therefore, we introduce the concepts of interference and workload for the purpose of investigation.

During time interval [a, b], there are m high-priority tasks being executed. At this moment, task τ i cannot be scheduled on any processor. While task τ i is in a waiting state, the execution time of high-priority tasks serves as interference. We use L i
div.formula: L i (a, b) = L k i (a, b) m , ∀i, k, a, b. (3
div.p: Within interval [a, b], the computational requirement of task τ i is represented by the workload M i (a, b). Baker's study indicates that the computation for M i (a, b) needs to consider the following three components (see Figure 1) [14]:

• carry-in: jobs arriving before time a and not completed before time a are referred to as carry-in jobs. The contribution of each job to the pair is denoted as E i . In general, we use real numbers to represent time instants and intervals. However, real-world time is not infinitely divisible. Time can only be precisely divided into the system's clock cycle. Therefore, we assume that any time value t is a non-negative integer and represents the entire interval [t, t+1).

Through this assumption, we can use mathematical induction on clock ticks for proofs. This approach avoids potential issues near endpoints and prevents impractical schedulability results based on the ability to divide time at arbitrary points.

div.head: C. BP-EDF scheduling
div.p: BP-EDF assigns priorities to tasks based on their absolute deadlines: tasks with earlier deadlines have higher priorities. We establish a global queue for executable tasks according to the global scheduling strategy [15]. BP-EDF permits preemptive task execution. In reality, preemption between tasks introduces additional overhead, which can lead to suboptimal system performance. Moreover, task preemption may introduce uncertainty, affecting the predictability of tasks. In our experiments, we will assess the extra overhead by evaluating the number of task preemptions.

The operation of the BP-EDF scheduling algorithm on a homogeneous multiprocessor is as follows: (1) When an active job is ready for execution and all processors are already allocated to other tasks; (2) When the number of active jobs is less than the number of processors, the jobs execute on the available processors; (3) When the number of active jobs exceeds the number of processors, high-priority tasks take precedence, and low-priority tasks wait for available processors; (4) High-priority tasks preempt low-priority tasks at appropriate preemption points.

The preemption strategy of the EP-EDF scheduling algorithm is that high-priority tasks preempt at the nearest preemption point. On the other hand, the preemption strategy of the LP-EDF scheduling algorithm is that high-priority tasks preempt at the preemption point of the lowest-priority task.

Under BP-EDF scheduling, if all jobs of a given task set can complete on time, then we consider the task set schedulable under BP-EDF. The schedulability test obtained in Section III for BP-EDF provides a guarantee of schedulability.

Example 1: Figure 2 illustrates an example of BP-EDF on a homogeneous multiprocessor platform. The upward-pointing arrows denote task arrival times, while the downward-pointing arrows represent task deadlines. Considering two processors Γ = {p 1 , p 2 } and four tasks Ω = {τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 , τ 4 }. Tasks τ 3 and τ 4 arrive before t 1 and are executed on each processor. At t 1 , τ 1 and τ 2 arrive exactly. Because tasks τ 1 and τ 2 have higher priority, they preempt processors p 1 and p 2 . t 2 is the preemption point of task τ 4 , the nearest preemption point, and the preemption point of the task with the lowest priority. In both EP-EDF and LP-EDF scheduling, task τ 1 preempts task τ 4 at t 2 . But the picture shows that τ 4 resumes execution after τ 1 completes. In this case, τ 4 will miss the deadline, that is, the task set is EP-EDF and LP-EDF unschedulable. If under BP-EDF scheduling, task τ 1 will preempt τ 3 at t 3 and task τ 2 will preempt τ 4 at t 4 . In this case, all tasks will not miss the deadline, that is, the task set is BP-EDF schedulable. To sum up, BP-EDF can schedule task sets in some cases. And these task sets cannot be scheduled by either EP-EDF or LP-EDF.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we implemented three different limitedpreemption EDF scheduling algorithms with distinct preemption strategies. We conducted extensive simulations to compare their performance. Additionally, we implemented the fully preemptive EDF (FP-EDF) as a reference for comparison. Our experiments varied the number of processors, the number of tasks, the system utilization, and the proportion of high-utilization tasks. We compared various metrics across different experiments, including the proportion of schedulable task sets and the number of task preemptions. The system utilization is defined as U sum /S sum . U sum is the sum of task utilizations, and S sum is the sum of processor speeds.

div.head: A. Experimental parameter setup
div.p: We conducted experiments on a homogeneous multiprocessor platform with various parameters, where D i = T i . Table II is the parameter range for each task. We generated 10,000 task sets based on the algorithm [17]. And each task set passed the feasibility test as described in [18]. Due to the existence of fixed preemption points, the execution of tasks is divided into several non-preemptive regions (NPRs). We set the length of each NPR to be no less than 10% of the task's execution time. Therefore, the number of fixed preemption points for each task will not exceed 9.

div.head: B. Evaluation of experiments
div.p: When m = 4, the experimental results are shown in Figure 5. We can observe that BP-EDF is capable of scheduling a larger proportion of task sets. Regardless of the system utilization rate, BP-EDF outperforms the other two strategies. At lower system utilization rates, all three different preemption strategies perform well. However, as the system utilization rate increases, the proportion of schedulable task sets decreases rapidly, eventually reaching 0. It's worth noting that because FP-EDF allows preemptions at any point, its better schedulability is evident. In practice, the preemption delay of FP-EDF is challenging to accurately calculate, which significantly impacts its performance. In practice, under any preemption, FP-EDF incurs significant and challenging-tocalculate preemption delays, which can adversely impact its performance. Both schedulability and preemption delay are crucial metrics for evaluating the effectiveness of an algorithm. It's necessary to consider both aspects when assessing algorithm performance.

When m = 8, the experimental results is Figure 6. The performance of BP-EDF remains superior. Despite the increase in the number of processors, we have also increased the number of tasks, where the number of tasks is n = 2(m + 1). Therefore, the experimental data is lower than that of the case when m = 4.

When m = 16, the experimental results are depicted in Figure 7. The experiment further corroborates the superior performance of BP-EDF, and the experimental data also declines further. It can be observed that when the system utilization reaches 60 -70%, the proportion of schedulable task sets for LP-EDF decreases to 0. For BP-EDF and EP-EDF as well, the proportion of schedulable task sets drops to 0 at 80 -90% system utilization.

We define tasks with utilization between 80-100% as highutilization tasks. In the earlier simulation experiments, the number of high-utilization tasks was not restricted. Because the system utilization remains constant, the proportion of high-utilization tasks affects the utilization of the remaining tasks. When the proportion of high-utilization tasks is high, the utilization of other tasks is constrained to very low levels, making such experiments meaningless. Therefore, we consider 30% to be a reasonable proportion. Now we set the high-utilization tasks to be 30%, and m = 8. In Figure 8, the schedulability for all three different preemption strategies further decreases. However, the schedulability of BP-EDF remains superior.

When m = 8, while keeping the total utilization of the task set constant, we vary the number of tasks. The experimental results are shown in Figure 9. Firstly, it's evident that BP-EDF maintains better schedulability. Secondly, with the increase in the number of tasks, the proportion of schedulable task sets also increases. This is because as the number of tasks increases, the proportion of tasks with low utilization within the task set also increases. Scheduling a larger number of tasks with low utilization is easier compared to scheduling a smaller number of high-utilization tasks, which is quite intuitive.

When m = 8, we conducted experiments to compare the number of task preemptions. In Figure 10, at different system utilizations, LP-EDF has the fewest task preemptions. BP-EDF has more preemptions than LP-EDF but fewer than EP-EDF. Additionally, the number of preemptions in BP-EDF is quite close to that of LP-EDF.

In summary, the schedulability performance of BP-EDF outperforms the other two algorithms in the experiments. BP-EDF can schedule the largest number of task sets under various conditions, including different system utilizations, processor counts, and high utilization task ratios. Furthermore, BP-EDF's task preemption count is also close to the bestperforming LP-EDF. Task preemption count directly impacts the predictability of tasks. Therefore, considering both schedulability and predictability, the applicability of BP-EDF is broader than LP-EDF and EP-EDF.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We have derived the schedulability test for BP-EDF and investigated three different preemption strategies of the EDF scheduling algorithm on a homogeneous multiprocessor platform. The experiments have shown that BP-EDF exhibits superior schedulability. LP-EDF demonstrates the least number of task preemptions, indicating lower preemption latency. However, BP-EDF's preemption count is close to that of LP-EDF. The study concludes that BP-EDF outperforms the other two processor allocation strategies in terms of schedulability and predictability. BP-EDF can be applied in a broader range of environments compared to the other two strategies.

In this paper, we have aimed to determine the most suitable preemption points for finite-preemption EDF scheduling. The purpose of this consideration is to minimize task preemption counts while ensuring schedulability remains unaffected. Through simulation experiments, we have observed that this approach of selecting optimal preemption points is highly effective. It guarantees algorithmic schedulability while reducing task preemption occurrences. BP-EDF not only employs the idea of selecting the nearest preemption point but also strives to minimize preemption counts while ensuring that the preemption of high-priority tasks does not cause missed deadlines for lower-priority tasks. As a result, BP-EDF can schedule a larger number of task sets compared to LP-EDF, and the preemption count is close to that of LP-EDF.
